title: Act III, Scene VI

teacherSummary.text: Lennox, speaking with heavy irony, lists the 'convenient' deaths and flights: how the 'right-valiant' Banquo walked too late, how Fleance must have killed his father because he fled, how wisely Macbeth killed the grooms. A Lord reports that Malcolm lives at the English court of the holy King Edward, that Macduff has gone to ask Edward to rouse Northumberland and Siward, and that Macbeth prepares for war.

context.history: Edward the Confessor (reigned 1042 to 1066) was revered as a saintly king; contrasting him with Macbeth sets holy kingship against tyranny.

significance: Public opinion turns: the thanes now speak of Macbeth as a tyrant. The scene shows how people talk under a dangerous ruler, in hints and irony.
discussionQuestions: Why might people use sarcasm or hints rather than speak plainly about someone in power?
Where does irony appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with guilt and conscience?

satQuestions.passage:
The son of Duncan,
From whom this tyrant holds the due of birth,
Lives in the English court, and is received
Of the most pious Edward with such grace
That the malevolence of fortune nothing
Takes from his high respect: thither Macduff
Is gone to pray the holy king, upon his aid
To wake Northumberland and warlike Siward:
That, by the help of these—with Him above
To ratify the work—we may again
Give to our tables meat, sleep to our nights,
Free from our feasts and banquets bloody knives,
Do faithful homage and receive free honours:
All which we pine for now: and this report
Hath so exasperate the king that he
Prepares for some attempt of war.
Sent he to Macduff?
He did: and with an absolute “Sir, not I,”
The cloudy messenger turns me his back,
And hums, as who should say “You’ll rue the time
That clogs me with this answer.”
And that well might
Advise him to a caution, to hold what distance
His wisdom can provide. Some holy angel
Fly to the court of England and unfold
His message ere he come, that a swift blessing
May soon return to this our suffering country
Under a hand accursed!
I’ll send my prayers with him.

segments.activity: Five key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Today's words: delinquents — offenders; bestows — lodges (himself); places; interpret — to explain the meaning of; accursed — under a curse; caution — a warning; care to avoid danger. “delinquents”: Origin of “delinquent”: Middle French délinquant; earlier Latin delinquens. “interpret”: Origin: probably Old French enterpreter; earlier Latin interpretor (“to explain”). “caution”: Origin: Old French caution (“security”); earlier Latin cautiō.

words.sentence:
How it did grieve Macbeth! did he not straight
In pious rage the two delinquents tear,
That were the slaves of drink and thralls of sleep?

But, peace! for from broad words and ’cause he fail’d
His presence at the tyrant’s feast, I hear
Macduff lives in disgrace: sir, can you tell
Where he bestows himself?

My former speeches have but hit your thoughts,
Which can interpret further: only, I say,
Things have been strangely borne.

Some holy angel
Fly to the court of England and unfold
His message ere he come, that a swift blessing
May soon return to this our suffering country
Under a hand accursed!

words.definition: a warning; care to avoid danger
words.sentence:
And that well might
Advise him to a caution, to hold what distance
His wisdom can provide.

segments.script: Edward the Confessor (reigned 1042 to 1066) was revered as a saintly king; contrasting him with Macbeth sets holy kingship against tyranny. Public opinion turns: the thanes now speak of Macbeth as a tyrant. The scene shows how people talk under a dangerous ruler, in hints and irony. Irony: Lennox speaks sarcastically about Duncan and Banquo's "deaths," exposing Macbeth's guilt. Characterization: Macduff has gone to England to seek help. Watch for kingship and order: Rightful kingship is tied to natural order; watch how disorder in the state shows up in nature.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Things have been strangely borne” slowly and put it in my own words: Talking with another lord, Lennox remarks that things have been strangely managed since Duncan's death. Next, craft. I notice his ironic understatement: he praises Macbeth on the surface while hinting at guilt underneath. The strongest word is “strangely”: it hints at suspicion without making an accusation that could get him killed. Then, effect. What is Lennox really saying when he calls events "strangely borne"? My answer: When Lennox calls events "strangely borne," he is really saying Macbeth arranged the murders of Duncan and Banquo; his careful sarcasm shows that the thanes now distrust Macbeth but fear to speak openly.
